interactions.summary: A student answers Jiang's embodiment question with mortality.
Jiang expands the answer into death, imperfection, and human capacity for evil, then pivots from human limitation to the Beatrice-Dante relationship.
A student identifies Beatrice and Dante as standing in a teacher-student relationship.
Jiang affirms the teacher-student model and asks whether Beatrice's answers are perfect, drawing agreement that she speaks absolute truth inside the poem.
A student complicates that claim by saying Beatrice's words are only an imperfect reflection of truth because Dante cannot yet receive truth directly.

Jiang restates the sequence step by step: Beatrice and Dante are teacher and student, Beatrice's understanding is perfect because she represents God, misunderstanding belongs to Dante, and the real question is why such teaching is needed at all.
A student answers that Dante is being taught so he can become a mouthpiece who tells others, and Jiang accepts the answer provisionally.

speaker_notes.note: The segment is mostly Jiang, but it also contains quick class affirmations, so it works better as an exchange than a pure monologue.
The diarization compresses Jiang's recap with scattered classroom confirmations into one long turn; the substantive argument still belongs to Jiang.

claims.claim: The class identifies mortality, death, imperfection, and the capacity for evil as features of human existence that distinguish humans from God.
The relationship between Beatrice and Dante is framed as teacher and student, with Dante asking and Beatrice answering.
A student argues that Beatrice's speech is an imperfect reflection of truth because the limitation lies in Dante's ability to receive what she knows.
Jiang insists that Beatrice's understanding of the universe is perfect because she represents God, even if Dante or readers misunderstand her words.
The point of teaching Dante is proposed as making him a mouthpiece who can carry what he has learned to other people.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang compresses the human difference from God into mortality, death, imperfection, and the ability to be evil.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Mortality. Death. Yes. Imperfection. Imperfection. Yes. We can be evil.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sharpens the embodiment turn by making human lack and danger the precondition for the next teaching argument.

signature_moments.moment: The student preserves Beatrice's authority while relocating imperfection into the medium of communication and Dante's capacity to receive it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: her words are but an imperfect reflection of the truth
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the packet its key interpretive distinction between perfect truth and imperfect transmission.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang refuses to let imperfect expression weaken Beatrice's status by insisting everything she says is perfect even if Dante misreads it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Everything she says is perfect. We may not understand what she says.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's cleanest statement of Jiang's split between divine truth and human reception.

signature_moments.moment: The lesson culminates in the idea that Dante is taught so he can become a human mouthpiece for truth rather than a private contemplative.
signature_moments.source_phrase: what then is the point of teaching Dante
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It converts the whole Beatrice-Dante exchange into a theory of imperfect but necessary human mediation.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The governing relationship Jiang uses to interpret Beatrice and Dante in this stretch of Paradiso.
A student's phrase for the gap between perfect truth and the limited human way Beatrice must communicate it to Dante.
The student's description of Dante as a human transmitter who receives instruction in order to tell other people.

chronology_notes.note: The packet moves from mortality and imperfection as distinctively human traits to a theory of why Dante still needs Beatrice's perfect teaching: not because truth is defective, but because a mortal human has to receive and retransmit it.

uncertainty_notes.note: Both long Jiang turns include brief classroom confirmations, but the argumentative content is clearly Jiang's rather than a balanced back-and-forth.
